summary.text: A 61-year-old right-handed man with prior right temporal and left temporo-occipital infarcts, residual quadrantanopia/mild amnesia and epilepsy on levetiracetam 500 mg retrospectively reported initial television-word incomprehension and radio-like noise at home, then presented with severe global aphasia and cortical deafness. Examination retained attention, pose imitation, normal muscle power and retained pain sensation and recurrent hearing/noise utterances. DWI excluded new lesions; FLAIR delineated old infarcts without vascular occlusion signs.

Initial IV diazepam 10 mg and phenytoin sodium 250 mg did not resolve symptoms; additional unspecified-dose phenytoin at 6 hours preceded sleep and partial recovery at 10 hours. Levetiracetam 1000 mg was used. EEG 10 hours showed 1 Hz left parieto-temporal periodic discharges and Day 1 SPECT left temporal/parietal high uptake. Speech seemed baseline by Day 5 with no EEG discharges; follow-up SPECT disappearance timing conflicts Day 6 body/Day 7 caption. Discharge was Day 7.

Two years later a similar attack with negative DWI was treated with IV diazepam 20 mg at 1 hour; partial recovery at 4 hours became complete aphasia/deafness recovery by Day 2 despite EEG periodic discharges. Gabapentin 1200 mg was added to levetiracetam; discharge Day 14. Seven years after the last attack he was independent without infarct or epileptic recurrence. Authors diagnose ASE with preserved consciousness; this is explicitly a patient re-reported from an earlier article.

She was also diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma four months earlier and was treated with osimertinib. At the same time, she was also diagnosed with metastatic brain tumors in the right cerebellar hemisphere and left occipital lobe on MRI (Figure 2A). She did not experience difficulties in conversation or daily life.

summary.text: An 80-year-old right-handed woman with epilepsy on levetiracetam 1000 mg and lung adenocarcinoma treated with osimertinib four months earlier had prior MRI brain metastases with conflicting body/caption site descriptions. A brief tonic-clonic seizure preceded severe aphasia. At 80 minutes spontaneous eye opening, normal power/pain and pose imitation were retained but repetition/naming/questions/commands were impaired. Initial CT was negative; after IV levetiracetam 500 mg the source literally reports a convulsive seizure.

Day 1 aphasia persisted despite preserved awareness and self-care. At 22 hours DWI showed no new infarcts, FLAIR no lesions including prior metastases, and EEG bilateral spike/wave complexes. NCSE was diagnosed; IV diazepam 5 mg gave immediate partial language recovery without sleep, and levetiracetam 1500 mg was used. Day 2 residual paraphasia/comprehension deficits and selective recall preceded complete recovery/negative EEG by Day 4; Day 5 SPECT still showed bilateral parietal high uptake. Rehabilitation transfer Day 6 was followed by discharge a month later and resumed living alone.

At 2.5 years she recurred with global aphasia without convulsions. Rapid IV diazepam 5 mg before imaging restored speech immediately; subsequent DWI remained negative and 6 hour EEG showed bilateral fronto-parieto-occipital discharges. Day 1 SPECT showed bilateral superior parietal/left frontal high uptake; lacosamide 100 mg was added to levetiracetam. Residual Day 2 deficits resolved by Day 4, with negative Day 3 EEG and selective recall. Discharge Day 8 preceded three-year freedom from seizures, infarcts, lung cancer and brain metastasis recurrence with independent daily life.

figures.caption_summary:
Figure 1
Neuroimaging of Case 1A: Diffusion-weighted imaging two hours after onset revealing no new lesions. B: Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging showing old infarcts in the right lateral temporo-parietal lobes that had spread to the transverse temporal gyrus (arrowheads) and subcortical white matter, including the acoustic radiation, and left medial temporo-occipital lobes (arrow). C: Electroencephalography at 10 hours after onset, revealing 1 Hz lateralized periodic discharges in the left parieto-temporal region. D: Single-photon emission computed tomography on Day 1, revealing a high-uptake lesion in the left superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyri and inferior parietal lobule (arrowheads). E: Follow-up single-photon emission computed tomography on Day 7 showing the disappearance of the high-uptake lesion that was observed on admission.
figures.attribution_notes: Explicit Case number in caption; text-only attribution. Conflicting timing/sites remain unresolved in facts, not pixel diagnoses.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 2
Neuroimaging of Case 2 at the first attackA: T1-weighted imaging four months before the first attack revealing well-enhanced lesions in the cerebellar vermis and bilateral occipital lobes, indicating metastatic tumors (arrows). B: Diffusion-weighted imaging 22 hours after onset, revealing no new lesions. C: Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging at 22 hours after onset showing no lesions, including metastatic lesions, which were observed four months ago. D: Electroencephalography at 22 hours after onset, revealing spike and wave complex in the bilateral whole brain. E: Single-photon emission computed tomography on Day 5, revealing a high-uptake lesion in the bilateral superior and inferior parietal lobules (arrows).
